title: Wishes and the Unreal Past
summary: Past forms with non-past meaning: wish, if only, it's time, would rather, as if, and the subjunctive after suggest and insist.

sections.heading: Wish and if only about the present
sections.body:
`wish` and `if only` followed by the past simple describe a present situation the speaker is dissatisfied with. The past tense is again a marker of unreality, not of past time: `I wish I lived closer to the campus` is a statement about today.

`If only` is the more emphatic of the two and often stands alone as an exclamation. With `be`, `were` is used for all persons in careful writing, though `was` is common and accepted in speech. Note also that these verbs take a negative in the clause to regret something that is true: `I wish I didn't have to commute`.

examples.right: I wish I lived closer to the campus.
examples.wrong: I wish I live closer to the campus.
examples.note: The present situation is regretted with a past simple, not a present.

examples.right: If only the report were shorter; nobody has time for ninety pages.
examples.note: Were is the careful form after wish and if only, and was is acceptable informally.

examples.right: She wishes she didn't have to teach on Fridays.
examples.note: The clause is negated to regret something that is in fact the case.

sections.heading: Wish and if only about the past
sections.body:
The past perfect after `wish` or `if only` expresses regret about something that did or did not happen earlier. It is one step further back than the past simple, and the difference in meaning is real: `I wish I studied medicine` regrets a present course of life, while `I wish I had studied medicine` regrets a decision taken years ago.

`could have` appears in the same slot when the regret concerns an unrealised ability or opportunity: `I wish I could have stayed longer`.

examples.right: I wish I had paid more attention in the statistics lectures.
examples.wrong: I wish I paid more attention in the statistics lectures last year.
examples.note: A past occasion, marked by last year, requires the past perfect.

examples.right: If only we had booked the tickets in September.
examples.note: Regret about a past omission, with the result still felt now.

examples.right: I wish I could have attended the closing session.
examples.note: Could have covers a past opportunity that was not available.

sections.heading: Wish plus would
sections.body:
`wish` + `would` is not simply another way of regretting the present. It complains about a repeated, irritating habit, or asks for a change in behaviour that lies outside the speaker's control: `I wish the neighbours would turn their music down`. Because it is a wish about somebody else's willingness, its subject is normally a different person, or an impersonal `it`.

This is why `I wish I would` fails. A speaker cannot ask for their own willingness to change, so English requires `I wish I could` for ability and `I wish I were` or the past simple for a state. Nor is `would` used for states that nobody can decide to alter: `I wish it would be sunny` is wrong where `I wish it were sunny` is right, though `I wish it would stop raining` is fine because the rain is an ongoing action.

examples.right: I wish the department would announce the timetable earlier.
examples.note: A complaint about somebody else's repeated behaviour.

examples.right: I wish I could concentrate for longer.
examples.wrong: I wish I would concentrate for longer.
examples.note: With the same subject, would is impossible; could expresses the missing ability.

examples.right: I wish it were warmer in this building.
examples.wrong: I wish it would be warmer in this building.
examples.note: Would needs a changeable action, not a state.

sections.heading: It's time and would rather
sections.body:
`It's time`, `It's high time` and `It's about time` are followed by a past simple when a subject is named: `It's time we left`. The meaning is present and mildly critical, implying that the action is overdue. The alternative with an infinitive, `It's time to leave`, names no subject and carries no criticism.

`would rather` works in two ways. With the same subject it takes a bare infinitive: `I'd rather work from home`. With a different subject it takes a past simple, on the same unreal-past principle: `I'd rather you worked from home`. For past preferences the pattern is `would rather have done`, and the comparison is completed with `than`, not `that`.

examples.right: It's high time the university reviewed its assessment policy.
examples.wrong: It's high time the university reviews its assessment policy.
examples.note: With a named subject, it's time takes the past simple.

examples.right: I'd rather you contacted the client yourself.
examples.wrong: I'd rather you contact the client yourself.
examples.note: A change of subject after would rather forces the past simple.

examples.right: She'd rather work from home than commute two hours a day.
examples.wrong: She'd rather to work from home than commute.
examples.note: Same subject, bare infinitive, and than to complete the comparison.

examples.right: I'd rather have taken the earlier flight.
examples.note: Would rather have done expresses a preference about the past.

sections.heading: As if and as though
sections.body:
`as if` and `as though` are interchangeable. When the comparison is clearly contrary to fact, they take an unreal past: a past simple for a present impossibility, a past perfect for a past one. `He speaks as though he owned the building` implies that he does not.

A present tense after `as if` is not an error; it signals that the speaker regards the comparison as possibly true. `It looks as if the talks have collapsed` reports a likely reading of the evidence. The choice of tense therefore carries meaning, and the past form should be reserved for what is known to be false.

examples.right: He talks about the merger as if it were already agreed, though nothing has been signed.
examples.note: The past form marks the comparison as false.

examples.right: She described the ruins as though she had excavated them herself.
examples.note: A past perfect for a past situation known not to have occurred.

examples.right: It looks as if the talks have collapsed.
examples.note: A present perfect because the speaker thinks this may well be true.

sections.heading: The subjunctive after suggest, insist and recommend
sections.body:
Verbs and nouns of proposing and requiring — `suggest`, `recommend`, `insist`, `demand`, `propose`, `request`, `urge`, and `it is essential/vital that` — are followed by a that-clause containing the bare infinitive, whatever the subject: `I suggest that he be informed`, `The board demanded that she resign`. There is no third-person `-s`, and the negative is formed with a bare `not`: `that he not be informed`.

Two alternatives are more common in everyday British usage. `should` may be inserted (`I suggest that he should be informed`), or the whole structure avoided with a noun or an `-ing` form (`I suggest informing him`). Note that `suggest` never takes an object plus infinitive: `I suggest you to check` is wrong.

examples.right: The committee recommended that the deadline be extended by two weeks.
examples.wrong: The committee recommended that the deadline is extended by two weeks.
examples.note: A mandative that-clause takes the bare infinitive, with no agreement and no tense.

examples.right: The auditor insisted that every transaction should be recorded in the ledger.
examples.note: Should plus infinitive is the ordinary British alternative to the subjunctive.

examples.right: I suggest checking the figures before you submit them.
examples.wrong: I suggest you to check the figures before you submit them.
examples.note: Suggest takes an -ing form or a that-clause, never an object plus to-infinitive.

examples.right: It is essential that the samples not be exposed to light.
examples.note: The subjunctive is negated with a bare not, without do.

slips: I wish I would is not English: use I wish I could for ability and I wish I were or a past simple for a state.
wish plus past simple regrets the present; wish plus past perfect regrets the past. I wish I knew is about now, I wish I had known is about then.
It's time takes a past simple once a subject appears: It's time we started, not It's time we start.
would rather changes form with the subject: I'd rather leave now but I'd rather you left now.
Complete a would rather comparison with than, not that or from: I'd rather walk than wait.
suggest and recommend never take an object plus to-infinitive: I recommend that you apply or I recommend applying, never I recommend you to apply.

questions.prompt: I wish I ___ more attention in the statistics lectures last year.
questions.explain: Last year fixes the regret in the past, and past regret after wish takes the past perfect. paid would regret a present habit instead.

questions.prompt: If only the report ___ shorter; nobody has the time to read ninety pages.
questions.explain: If only plus a past simple expresses dissatisfaction with the present; were is preferred in formal writing but was is accepted.

questions.prompt: I wish the neighbours ___ their music down after midnight; they keep it on until three every night.
questions.explain: Wish plus would complains about somebody else's repeated behaviour and asks for a change. turned would describe a hypothetical state rather than the recurring nuisance the second clause names.

questions.prompt: It's high time the university ___ its assessment policy; the current one dates from 2009.
questions.explain: It's time with a named subject takes the past simple, implying that the action is already overdue.

questions.prompt: I wish I ___ better at public speaking, because I have a viva next week.
questions.explain: A wish about one's own present state takes the past form of be. would cannot be used with the same subject, since it asks for a willingness to change that lies with somebody else.

questions.prompt: I wish I ___ the earlier train; the meeting had already started when I arrived.
questions.explain: The regret concerns a completed past action, so the past perfect is required after wish.

questions.prompt: I'd rather you ___ the client yourself; my German isn't good enough for a negotiation.
questions.explain: Would rather takes a past simple when the subject of the preference changes. The bare infinitive is correct only when both subjects are the same, as in I'd rather contact him.

questions.prompt: She'd rather ___ from home than commute two hours a day.
questions.hint: work (form after would rather, same subject)
questions.explain: With one subject throughout, would rather is followed by a bare infinitive, and the comparison is completed with than plus a second bare infinitive.

questions.prompt: She described the ruins as though she ___ them herself, though she has never left the country.
questions.explain: The final clause shows the comparison is impossible, and an unreal past situation after as though takes the past perfect. has excavated would present it as probably true.

questions.prompt: The auditor insisted that every transaction ___ recorded in the ledger on the day it took place.
questions.hint: be (subjunctive; the should form is also accepted)
questions.explain: After insist, demand and recommend the that-clause takes a bare infinitive, with should plus infinitive as the common British alternative.

questions.prompt: The committee recommended that the deadline ___ extended by two weeks.
questions.explain: Mandative verbs take a subjunctive that-clause with no agreement and no tense marking. is extended turns the proposal into a report of fact.

questions.prompt: It's high time something ___ about the state of the cycle lanes.
questions.explain: It's high time is followed by a past form even though the meaning is present and urgent; the passive simply becomes was done.
